headline: Partner at PwC - Specializing in Cybersecurity and Risk
about:
Kelly is a Principal in PwC’s Advisory Practice, based in Chicago, where she is a leader in the Firm’s Cybersecurity, Risk and Regulatory practice. With more than 25 years of experience in information security and cyber/tech risk management, she understands the cyber threat and risk landscape and how to help companies both manage that risk and enable their business. Leveraging that insight, Kelly specializes in helping organizations take a risk-based approach to asset protection and enterprise resiliency guiding executive teams on how to effectively focus the limited resources available on the initiatives that will bring the most value.  Kelly is often sought after to lead teams through the intricacies of enterprise transformation efforts involving the development and execution of strategies focused on modernizing the cyber function, the design and implementation of solutions, such as identity and access management and information protection, as well as, developing new target operating models that involve updated policies, standards, and re-engineered processes.

Working across a diverse portfolio of companies, Kelly also frequently advises Boards and executive teams on the ever changing regulatory landscape as it relates to cybersecurity.  She often works with her clients and leads teams to both assess compliance against cybersecurity regulations, such as FFIEC, NY DFS, NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) Framework, NAIC cybersecurity principles, and OCC’s Heightened Standards, and assist with obtaining compliance.

Kelly is passionate about women in technology and cybersecurity and spends her time sponsoring and developing the next generation of female leaders both at PwC and in the market.  She helped found the initial Women in Technology inclusion group at PwC and participates with external groups such as Executive Women’s Forum (EWF) and Women in Cybersecurity (WiCyS).

experience.description:

Advises Boards of Directors and executive teams on how to become compliant with emerging laws/regulations focused on IT and Cybersecurity enhancements, as well as, designing and managing the program to help achieve compliance

Leads teams, in response to a data breach, for example, that designs and develops data analytics solutions geared towards analyzing who has access to what system/data in an effort to minimize insider threat

projects.title: Computers and Computing Project
projects.description:
This project was to create a website for a company in need of a web developer.

When starting the project, I was able to design a web page for an imaginary company, or a real company that I would want to start up. The company had to be a not-for-profit, a service company, or a for-profit enterprise. I chose to build a website for a golf pro shop.

My job was to inform the world about my enterprise. I created a products and about page for the pro shop equipment and the employee information. All extra pages linked back to my home page which included information on the company's history.

I used XHTML to provide the structure and dictate the content of my pages. A CSS page was used to take care of all formatting, e.g., font selection, size and color, background color, positioning, etc.

projects.title: Informatics Group Project
projects.description:
This project's theme was based on this year's Microsoft Imagine Cup student competition. In the competition, students around the world are invited to use their skills, imagination, and passion to create a technology solution that addresses each year's theme.

This year’s theme: Imagine a World Where Technology Helps Solve the Toughest Problems.

In this team based assignment, I had the privilege of working with two other classmates. The goal of the project was to work together as a team and use technology to solve a problem of our choice from around the world.

In response to answering the projects main question, my teammates and I began by going through the process of defining our problem, researching, and creating a preliminary concept. We did not have to program or complete our final design, but did focus on creating a realistic solution. Our concept could have been anything from a website to a phone app or to a completely original information system, as long as it somehow connected to technology. The concept that my group and I ended up with was a video game, which teachers and students alike could use in the classroom. We believed that our concept addressed the issues of students not receiving enough hands on experience in the educational subject of science.This issue can be seen as a serious one because without any change students might experience huge gaps in their basic knowledge.

Once we had selected our group problem and mutually agreed on a concept, we began conducting research, gathering data, and developing a proposed video game based on our research and data. Ultimately, our group ended up developing a final website to display all of the information collected including our research, data, and solution. During the last week of class before winter break we presented the problem, and the proposed solution that included a realistic graphic of our prototype.

headline: Director Consulting Services at PwC
about:
I am an innovator and analytical problem solver at heart, and that is what drove me to pursue my education as a mechanical engineer. I obtained my BS and MS degree in Mechanical Engineering from Northwestern University as a 5 year fast track program offered by the university. Upon graduation I moved from my Midwestern roots in the northwestern suburbs of Chicago to start a new adventure in Houston with HP. In the last 6 years I have changed roles from a thermal engineer to a mechanical engineer specialist and witnessed various corporate reorganizations. Looking to further expand my horizons and in the interest of continued learning I enrolled in Fuqua's CCMBA program in July 2016 with a planned completion date of December 2017. The international exposure and team-based structure is what attracted me to the CCMBA program. 

My educational background in mechanical engineering is in design and manufacturing, with exposure to micro- and nano-technologies. Additionally, during my undergraduate and master's degree studies at NU I pursued a background in business and management, with an undergraduate minor in Business Institutions, and a graduate minor in Engineering Management. 

I began my career working as a summer intern for 5 years with Motorola Mobile Devices in both mechanical design and software development. With my experience in product development, design, and manufacturing, as well as being a lead engineer with responsibilities including schedule and cost optimization, I have striven to garner a career focused on using practical experience to drive business outcomes and deliver successful solutions to industry issues. 

Specialties: • Engineering: design and manufacturing, structural analysis, manufacturing, composite materials, MEMS/Nanotechnology
• Strategy: new product development, project management
• Computer Software: ProEngineer, Unigraphics NX, SolidWorks, Optistruct, Microsoft Office Suite
• Computer Programming: MATLAB, LabVIEW, Basic

about:
Brad is a Partner in PwC’s greater Chicago practice.   In this role, he leads the audit process for public SEC registrants as well as privately held companies and he focusses on the fundamentals of high quality client service.  His areas of specialty include SEC reporting, SOX, business combinations, impairments, segment reporting, discontinued operations, consolidation and equity accounting. 

In addition, Brad serves as a Partner in PwC's Alliance with Workiva.  In this role, he helps client's maximize efficiencies in financial reporting and integrated risk management.  

Brad previously served in PwC's National Office, assisting Partners and Managers with accounting technical consultations and thought leadership. He is a Certified Public Accountant (CPA), licensed to practice in Illinois and Wisconsin and a member of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants.  Additionally Brad is a Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) and is Workiva Platform Certified.

about:
Over the past 20 years at PwC, I’ve had the privilege of guiding private equity and corporate clients through acquisition, divestiture and joint venture. Today, I’m proud to serve as the Deals Leader for PwC US and Mexico, building on my previous roles as Private Equity Leader and Deputy Deals Leader.  

I’ve had a particular focus on healthcare clients – from pharma, life sciences, medical devices, hospitals, to healthcare IT – supporting transactions ranging from $5M to $2B. I’m passionate about working with clients who are eager to push the edge of what’s possible in deals and value creation. 
 
Private equity has been a major focus throughout my career. I’ve worked closely with firms to help instill a cash culture, improve portfolio company performance, and deliver flawless transactions. At PwC, we bring an integrated approach that draws on our deep PE experience to anticipate challenges across the fund and portfolio lifecycle — making the complex world of private equity a little simpler and helping clients capture opportunity. 
 
Outside of work, I’m a proud husband and father of two children. Between work and children’s sporting events on the weekends, there isn’t much time left for personal hobbies! But as a family, we enjoy time together outside, hiking and soaking up all that the arts community in Chicago has to offer.  
 
You can learn more about me and PwC by clicking on the links in the ‘Featured’ section. If I can be of any assistance, please do not hesitate to reach out via LinkedIn.

publications.title: PwC Customer Loyalty Executive Survey 2023: Converting disconnects into loyalty opportunities
publications.description:
As companies continue to navigate market volatility, securing and expanding their relationships with their customers is perhaps more important than ever. Short-term pressures such as inflation and uncertain supply chains can push some leaders to reactively focus only on retention. But if you don’t understand how your customers make loyalty decisions throughout their journey with your brand, your business won’t be able to turn loyalty into real growth.

PwC surveyed more than 400 executives who are either responsible for or share influence regarding customer loyalty or retention decisions. We wanted to learn how well their companies are capitalizing on customer loyalty opportunities as they address current challenges. The PwC Customer Loyalty Executive Survey 2023 followed our May 2022 survey of more than 4,000 consumers in the United States. Taken together, the two surveys can help illustrate openings, moments and other pivotal points when you can increase customer engagement with your brands and improve the chances that they’ll not only stay but develop deeper bonds that turn loyalty into a growth engine.

publications.title: Creating loyalty in volatile times
publications.description:
Volatility in consumer behavior is at an all-time high. The COVID-19 pandemic fundamentally changed many needs and preferences. Inflation and a turbulent economy are influencing buying decisions. Technology creates unprecedented connectivity and access to goods and services. Consumers know more about where companies stand on environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues and expect businesses to share their beliefs. And let’s be honest: Consumers as a whole are more discerning than ever.

This all leaves companies wondering how they can better shape consumer demand and drive engagement with their brands. Unlocking what drives consumer loyalty has companies asking, “How do I attract and retain my customers?” Along with providing new insights from more than 4,000 consumers in the US, our PwC Customer Loyalty Survey 2022 reveals several opportunities for businesses to strengthen relationships, increase customer lifetime value and reduce the likelihood that they’ll leave.

publications.title: Bring your shades. The future looks bright
publications.description:
What will the future look like for travel after the abrupt standstill in early 2020? With vaccinations on the rise and infections on the decline in the US, a growing number of consumers are eager to get away. Many have the financial wherewithal, having been hunkered down at home for much of the past year, with fewer-than-usual opportunities to spend money. 

Despite this enthusiasm, many travel companies are struggling to visualize—and shape—the future of travel, recognizing that they need to acknowledge newly formed consumer expectations for trips to the mountains, the beach or the boardroom.

To understand the latest shifts in travel expectations, attitudes and behaviors—as well as the sustainability of those shifts—PwC surveyed more than 1,300 US consumers in April 2021 and compared the results to earlier surveys conducted in April and August of 2020. Most respondents to our latest survey told us they have at least one flight and/or an overnight stay planned for business or leisure within the next 12 months.

publications.title: Travelers on the move again
publications.description:
The travel industry is gradually moving again, but predicting travel demand is challenging in a rapidly changing environment. For now, self-quarantine measures required when traveling from high risk areas continue to keep most would-be travelers homebound. The good news: Once consumers take that first trip in this new environment, they are far more willing to travel again. However, a number of other factors — most of which stem from uncertainty — could continue to influence consumer travel behavior.

To stay current with evolving expectations, attitudes and behaviors about travel, PwC surveyed more than 1,000 consumers nationwide during the week of July 8, 2020, following an earlier survey conducted in April. All respondents had taken at least one flight or spent at least one night in a hotel in 2019.

publications.title: How to restore confidence in travel during an uncertain time
publications.description:
Safety is top of mind for consumers as they look beyond the current shelter-in-place mandates toward a recovery period when they can resume traveling. What else are they looking for beyond safety? What sources do they trust for information? What reassurances do they need when they travel?

To find out about expectations, attitudes and behaviors, PwC surveyed more than 1,000 consumers nationwide during the week of April 22. All respondents had taken at least one flight or spent at least one night in a hotel during 2019.

publications.title: Simplifying the Business - 2017 (New Ideas: Personalization)
publications.description:
The IATA Simplifying the Business (StB) program is a transformative driver of innovation through key projects and initiatives that aim to improve the passenger experience. Led by a group of innovation-focused airline representatives that are key transformers within their proper organizations, StB has become a cornerstone of innovation in IATA and across the industry

New Idea #3 - Personalization: 
Personalization has been at the forefront of travel sales, service, and delivery for over twenty years, but the technology needed to deliver personalization at scale is only just reaching
maturity. With strategic coordination between members of the travel ecosystem on the use of traveler data and clear standards for its management and application, the travel industry has the opportunity to deliver on the longstanding promise of a truly personalized travel experience.

publications.title: Digital operating models: How leading companies achieve results in the digital world
publications.description:
For this report, we identified a dozen global companies that have cracked the digital code—turning high-level talk about digital strategy into meaningful, high-quality, operational action across the enterprise in a consistent, fast, and predictable way. These companies are globally located and span major industry sectors, including consumer goods, travel and hospitality, financial services,
healthcare, and retail. Our goal was to learn from these digital exemplars and identify the leading 
 practices of a digital operating model.

headline: Principal Mergers & Acquisitions Tax Group  at PwC
about:
Shawn Hussein is a principal in the Mergers & Acquisitions ("M&A") Tax practice in Philadelphia, PA. 

Prior to joining the Philadelphia M&A Tax practice, Shawn was a director in the Washington National Tax Services ("WNTS") M&A Tax Practice within PwC. WNTS is the technical core of PwC's tax practice. The WNTS M&A Tax practice is a premier, highly experienced team, including former senior Congressional, Treasury, and IRS officials, that assists companies in staying up to date on the latest legislative, regulatory, and judicial matters, and helps companies navigate the ever-changing tax landscape. The PwC WNTS M&A Tax team delivers innovative tax advice on some of the largest and most complex corporate transactions. 

Shawn's practice focuses advising on tax-free reorganizations, spin-offs and similar transactions, the cross-border implications of corporate transactions, redemption transactions, global restructurings, and taxable acquisitions. In addition, Shawn's expertise focuses on the preservation of tax attributes (including U.S. federal net operating losses). Shawn has performed numerous Section 382 studies on both public and privately held corporations throughout many different industries. 

Shawn obtained his Master of Laws in Taxation from the University of Miami School of Law, his Juris Doctor from Duquesne University School of Law, and his Bachelor of Arts from the Pennsylvania State University. Shawn is also licensed to practice law in the state of Pennsylvania.

publications.description: GenAI, data science and a broad appetite for analytics has been out of the shadows for a while now, and carriers now have to find ways to democratize their data.  But there’s a big problem. Data remains virtually unusable in layer upon layer of systems, sprawling and disconnected. There is no enterprise data model.  The leap from a complex, ad hoc, ungoverned world to one of order and trust is hard for many carriers to fathom. Ultimately, they have to decide that they can’t endure the pain of being an invertebrate anymore and commit to having a backbone – an enterprise data backbone

publications.title: Out with the many: Redesigning distributor compensation as a shared service
publications.description:
Cutting costs, tapping transparency

Insurance carriers today are wondering: How can they lower fixed costs? Meanwhile, their distribution partners are looking for greater transparency and ease of doing business. We maintain that by addressing fragmented legacy operating environments, carriers can address both of these challenges.

The typical multi-line insurance carrier today maintains many different systems to pay compensation to distribution partners, usually as a result of M&A activity without subsequent consolidation. As a result, when partners deal with multiple business units across the company, their experience is inconsistent and disjointed. These partners are now demanding an improved experience, and arguably the most important touchpoint between a carrier and its partners is compensation.

publications.title: BPO for the Life & Annuity market
publications.description:
Life and annuity insurers are focusing on three areas to drive growth: distribution, product and brand. Growth is hard enough in today’s market, but it’s even harder when your back office holds you back, both in terms of fixed costs and limited capabilities. Accordingly, achieving operational efficiency is table stakes for life & annuity insurers competing in an extended soft market.  

Fortunately, given recent advances in technology and expansion of provider capabilities, business process outsourcing (BPO) has become a feasible way to reduce costs and increase efficiencies. Based on what we’ve seen in the market, we think BPO providers are ready to move from their traditional role as vendors to true business partner.  With scale, advanced technology,
and money to invest, the best of them offer great opportunity for insurers to significantly lower costs and benefit from complementary services over the long term.

publications.title: What's the Problem with 'best practices'?
publications.description:
In our recent non-scientific sampling of top U.S and Global personal lines and commercial lines executives, representing the entire gamut of functional areas, we asked – what’s the problem with best practices? We listened to their struggles and heard some success stories as well. 
Risk Manager’s strive toward best practices, and it’s a long hard road.

publications.title: Simplicity is the Ultimate Sophistication: How Life Insurers Can Streamline Incentive Compensation for their Producers
publications.description:
The complex web of compensation schedules that has evolved over time is reaching a critical mass. The demand for simplicity and transparency in producer compensation is arising from demographic, industry, and regulatory factors.

We have observed carriers struggling with a proliferation of schedules and incentives that are not aligned with strategy, while leading carriers are establishing the flexibility to craft compensation that aligns with corporate goals. Once this flexibility is established, carriers are better able to distinguish themselves from competitors in agents’ eyes. In our view, carriers should reduce the overall number of plans offered before replacing the underlying systems supporting incentive compensation. Without simplification before system transformation, carriers will re-platform legacy problems and miss out on many possible benefits.

publications.title: Underwriting Due Diligence Roadmap for Insurance M&A
publications.description: To limit potential underwriting leakage post-deal, it is important to thoroughly assess underwriting functions and capabilities pre-deal. Ideally this would be done through a multi-dimensional, holistic evaluation model that thoroughly assesses insurance underwriting functions. We describe below an example of such a model, which includes seven dimensions, each of which is further subdivided into granular, standalone components.

about:
As an AWS Cloud Infrastructure Engineer, I thrive on solving complex challenges and empowering businesses to fully harness the potential of cloud technology. With a proven track record in designing, deploying, and managing scalable, high-availability systems on AWS, I specialize in delivering impactful, tailored solutions that align with diverse business goals.

I have played a pivotal role in architecting robust AWS infrastructures by configuring VPCs, subnets, route tables, and internet gateways to build secure and efficient network architectures. Utilizing services like Elastic Load Balancing, Auto Scaling, EC2, RDS, and S3, I ensure optimal performance, high availability, and cost efficiency for my clients.

Security and compliance are at the heart of my work. I implement rigorous access controls using IAM policies, security groups, and NACLs, while leveraging tools such as Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail to maintain visibility and integrity across systems.

I’m deeply passionate about automation and DevOps practices. I excel in building and managing CI/CD pipelines using tools like GitHub, Jenkins, SonarQube, Prometheus, and Nexus, ensuring seamless code integration, thorough quality assurance, and efficient deployment processes.
Additionally, I bring extensive expertise in Kubernetes (EKS), including provisioning EKS clusters with self-managed nodes and managing deployments to support scalable, resilient, and containerized applications.

Also, I am experienced in Vendor Security Assessment, Network Design, and Vulnerability Management and I possess in-depth knowledge of standards and frameworks including ISO 27001/27002, NIST, CIS, CCM, PCI DSS, GDPR, etc. My skills in security privacy controls and assessments are complemented by a proven track record of delivering exceptional risk management support. Resilient, data-driven, self-motivated, and passionate about continuous learning and development, I am committed to advancing cybersecurity practices and enhancing organizational security. By combining technical excellence with a forward-thinking approach, I enable businesses to innovate, scale, and achieve their goals with cutting-edge cloud solutions.

headline: Deals Partner at PwC
about:
I am a Chicago based Deals Partner focused on helping clients identify and execute on the deals that accelerate their business strategy and generate value now and into the future.  I advise clients on the accounting and financial reporting complexity that arises throughout the deal cycle for acquisitions, carve-out divestitures and spin-off transactions as well as capital markets activities including IPOs and high yield debt offerings.  

I have over twenty-eight years of experience providing both core attestation and accounting advisory services to clients in a variety of industries with a focus on industrial products, pharma life sciences and retail and consumer markets. 
 
From November 2012 until June 2015, I was based in Frankfurt, Germany and led a team focused on US bound IPOs and registered capital raisings, 144a private placements and cross-border M&A transactions with a US element for clients across Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Belgium. 

From 2006 through 2008, I was deployed to the PwC practice in Moscow, Russia where I was responsible for the audits of large, complex clients--both U.S. domestic companies with operations in Russia, as well as Russian based firms with multi-national operations that prepare their financial statements in accordance with IFRS.  

Prior to 2006, I was a part of PwC’s core assurance team serving as the lead manager on key audit clients across multiple industry sectors and was integrally involved in the initial and go forward compliance efforts of my clients with the requirements of the Sarbanes-Oxley legislation.

I received my BS in Accounting from the University of Kansas and am a member of the AICPA.

Specialties: Refer to summary above.

headline: Accelerator of transformation and new ways of working
about:
Christopher Hannegan is a principal in PwC's Workforce Solutions practice and leads the firm's Organization & Talent offering, working with companies across industry sectors to accelerate transformation and new ways of working with a focus on leadership, organizational culture and effective communications. A journalist by training, his 32-year career has spanned in-house roles at Bayer, and management consulting firms and communications firms, including Strategy& and Edelman. He is the U.S. partner lead for PwC’s Katzenbach Center for Culture and Leadership.​

His notable work includes diagnosing cultural barriers to strategy execution at a global financial services firm, improving the risk and control environments at multiple banks, delivering a leadership development program for a professional services firm's top 4,000 leaders to drive growth, and designing fit-for-future corporate communications teams for multiple organizations. He also has worked with a Fortune 5 organization to adopt new ways of working, with a global airline to increase supervisor effectiveness and leadership connection to the front line, and with a leading bank to engage a global workforce around a transform

Christopher earned his B.A. in Journalism from Penn State University and has also completed foreign language studies at Christian Albrecht University in Kiel, Germany. He is highly proficient in German and operates comfortably across cultures and geographies. 

He lives with his husband in Chicago.

experience.description: Lead for the firm's Organization & Talent offering, including workforce strategy and organizational design, talent, culture and leadership, and enterprise learning.

Led the firm's employee engagement practice globally and co-led the firm's inclusion and diversity practice in the United States; provided strategic counsel to clients in support of transactions, crises, transformations, business strategy shifts and cultural evolutions; helped companies chart a path to better connecting with their workforces through more dynamic, creative and socially enabled communications approaches and programs; and build communications functions that deliver new value to the business.

experience.position: Executive Vice President & U.S. Practice Lead, Employee Engagement
experience.description:
Led $15+ million client practice of 50 employee engagement consultants and served as senior lead to firm’s marquee employee engagement clients to help them improve engagement and communications, manage change, increase leader and manager alignment, embed culture, and plan for complex events including M&A, business transformation, workforce reductions. 

Continually developed and refined employee engagement service offering to stay ahead of Edelman’s competitive set and be connected to future trends in technology, social media, employee advocacy, organizational design, leadership and content creation.

Established and led $10 million practice of 30 consultants focused on people and change issues for commercial clients undergoing transformation. Scope of work included strategic communications, change management, talent management and learning.

For major clients across a variety of industry sectors, played lead senior role in creating change and communications programs, including assessment, design, tactical planning and implementation.

Provided thought leadership in areas of strategic communications and change management to C-level clients and authored white papers to further firm’s external credibility in these areas.

Built and ran a client service offering focused on employee engagement and communications, achieving consistently high rates of growth and profit.

Designed and implemented employee engagement strategies for numerous national and global clients. Coached CEOs and other senior management on improving communications effectiveness. 

Conducted best practice benchmarking to identify industry trends in employee engagement, communications and use of social media.

Developed and executed client programs at this premium, boutique strategy execution firm for leadership communications, labor relations, bankruptcy filings, M&A activity, product launches, cost reduction efforts and business strategy shifts.

Designed and launched award-winning employee engagement initiatives to strengthen the relationship between senior management and front-line employees. Developed and implemented communications and leadership programs to drive culture change.

Executed a wide array of internal and external communications, including organization of and support for press conferences and special events, M&A communications, and overall strategic planning.

Youngest employee ever to be given foreign assignment in Germany. Three-year role focused on approving and facilitating communications strategies at Bayer AG subsidiaries in North America, including merger and acquisition work, internal communications, media relations, investor relations activity and crisis management.

Coached board members and other senior executives on effective communications approaches. 
Managed production of annual reports, corporate social responsibility reports and corporate brochures, including writing, photography, design, approval, production and distribution.

Developed, managed and implemented all communications and leadership activities for a major corporate identity rollout, including employee, customer, media and community events, as well as TV advertising. Managed advertising production budget of $1.3 million.

Enhancing the Yelp User Experience:
Explored several use cases utilizing Yelp review data, including developing a content-based recommendation engine and a text-based star generator in order to enhance end-user experience. To do so, we queried using Hive and developed a pipeline to apply various NLP methods (tokenization, Word2Vec) using Spark ML and Spark SQL.

Intensive Care Unit Patient Outcome Predictions:
Developed several machine learnings models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) in Python to best predict a patient’s survival within 24 hours of admission to a hospital Intensive Care Unit based on patient history and post-admission clinical data. Data was imbalanced, so we utilized random undersampling and sample minority oversampling technique to improve the models.

Drug and Clinical Trial Discovery Tool:
Developed an interactive tool that connects cancer patients to potential drugs and clinical trial treatment options based on patient-specific gene mutation, cancer type, and cancer stage for several prevalent cancer diagnoses in the US. Cleaned and transformed over 1 million patient records in a custom ETL pipeline, collected using Web-APIs with Python from different sources. Developed an interactive dashboard where patients find actively recruiting clinical trials based on their individual diagnosis type and stage.

I spent my collegiate years studying at Indiana University where I studied marketing and international business along with Spanish. I continued on there to study information systems through the MSIS program, which led me to my opportunity at PwC. 

Before choosing PwC, I was stuck between two pathways that would dictate the start of my career. One followed family traditions and the other was a relatively new path, unknown to my family and in a new state. I chose the less familiar path and moved to Chicago to begin my career at PwC in the Experience Center.

While I chose to move back to Indianapolis in the midst of the pandemic, my career at PwC has remained strong and passionate. 

At this firm, I curate my own life and my career. 
I work in collaborative forums with unique individuals and clients.
I connect with others genuinely and maintain strong relationships.
I learn from others while also teaching and mentoring others as well.
I embrace change and adapt quickly.
I bring my values to work and am involved in platforms that represent who I am.

I create amazing user experiences through sophisticated strategy and inclusive design.

The American College of Healthcare Executives is an international professional society of more than 48,000 healthcare executives who lead hospitals, healthcare systems and other healthcare organizations. ACHE's mission is to advance its members and healthcare leadership excellence.

In addition to membership, become a recognized leader among executives in healthcare management by becoming a Fellow of the American College of Healthcare Executives (FACHE). headline: Consultant, intelligence, thought leadership
about:
Trine Tsouderos is a communications and intelligence executive with expansive experience producing forward-looking analysis and insights, particularly for US health industries. In 2023, Tsouderos was Senior Vice President of Intelligence at Vizient and Sg2. For nearly a decade, Tsouderos worked for Health Research Institute, PwC's independent healthcare think tank. Tsouderos was one of the founders and original co-hosts of PwC's healthcare podcast, Next in Health, which continues to be produced to this day.

A former journalist, Tsouderos has 17 years of newsroom experience. She was a science and medical reporter at the Chicago Tribune, winning state and national awards for her work. Her work has been cited in books and scientific papers. Tsouderos lives outside Chicago with her husband, two children, and a Bernese Mountain Dog.

publications.title: Health reform 2.0 A guide to developing resilience amid an uncertain future for the Affordable Care Act
Surviving seismic change: Winning a piece of the $5 trillion US health ecosystem
publications.description: Where is the US health industry heading over the next 10 years? Which forces are reshaping the industry, how fast are they moving and how will they impact health organizations, both new and established? How has care changed – or not changed – for American health consumers?

publications.title: The pharmacy of the future: Hub of personalized health
publications.description: Retail pharmacies face shrinking margins in their core business and tougher competition in a shifting health industry. Yet these companies have the opportunity to redefine themselves as central players – and critical partners – in the New Health Economy.To paint a portrait of the present and future of retail pharmacies, PwC’s Health Research Institute (HRI) interviewed executives from Fortune 50 drugstore companies, big box retailers, supermarket chains, startups, prescription benefit managers and others. What emerged is a picture of an industry at a crossroads, but with three strategic opportunities: Become a health hub for consumers, deliver new value to traditional partners and new entrants and master the “last mile” to meet consumers where they are both virtually and physically.

publications.title: The coming plug-and-play health ecosystem
publications.description:
The health industry has long been a closed and highly-siloed system.
But powerful global forces are transforming the industry into a
nimble, innovative and modular ecosystem serving the consumer,
with profound implications for players new and traditional.

publications.title: Money matters: Payment and billing for a New Health Economy
publications.description: The nation's healthcare billing and payment system is an artifact of an earlier age. Much can be done to improve the system in the short term, but in the long term, structural change is needed. In this report, HRI diagnoses the billing and payment system, and prescribes short- and long-term solutions.

publications.title: The Future of Health Is More, Better, Cheaper
publications.description: Within a decade, the health business will look and feel like other consumer-oriented, technology-enabled industries. Soon, it will have its own Amazon.com-style, iconic, new economy brands—companies that can give consumers an easy way to access information, doctors, and treatments; provide them with a variety of services and products for a variety of prices; and centralize their care through user-friendly interfaces. And thanks to this growing trend, there are plenty of new entrants into the market who would like nothing better than to upend the old model of care and empower consumers, while taking some of the industry’s US$2.9 trillion market share for themselves.

publications.title: Top health industry issues of 2015
publications.description: Every year, PwC's Health Research Institute names the top issues that will shape the US healthcare industry in the coming year. This year, DIY healthcare, a drive for partnerships and the tension between convenience and security for health data are among the top issues. Read more in HRI's annual report.

publications.title: Health wearables: Early days
publications.description: While the smartphone remains Americans’ device of choice, the tech world is creating a future of wearable technology that promises to entertain consumers, save them money and help them live healthier lives. Technology companies’ interests in health and wellness have sparked the creation of a myriad of wearable devices, from fitness bands that monitor activity and sleep patterns   to flexible patches that can detect body temperature, respiration rate, hydration level, blood pressure and more.

publications.title: Healthcare's new entrants:  Who will be the industry's Amazon.com
publications.description: The health sector’s center of gravity is shifting toward consumers and new tech-savvy players are moving fast to capitalize on the change. These new entrants are poised to shake up the industry, drawing billions of dollars in revenue from traditional healthcare organizations while building lucrative new markets in the burgeoning New Health Economy.

projects.title: Project Run With It
projects.description:
Project Run With It (PRWI) furthers the community service component of Beta Alpha Psi and provides members/candidates with an opportunity to engage in a real-world consulting project.

As Beta Alpha Psi celebrates its 100th year anniversary, PRWI begins its 12th year with exciting news! There has been such a positive response from student participants and the nonprofit organizations served that we have decided to expand the competition and allow more students the opportunity to be involved. PRWI 2019 will involve up to 96 BAP student representatives working together during the annual meeting to develop solutions to real-life business problems of actual not-for-profit (NFP) organizations located in the greater Chicago, IL area. Working in teams of four, students will have the equivalent of one and half working days to develop a formal presentation showcasing their solution to the business issues presented by the NFPs in their request for proposal for consulting services. In 1998, Sheri earned a Bachelor of Science degree from University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, majoring in Accountancy.  She became a Certified Public Accountant in 1999.  Then in 2003, she completed the Master of Science in Taxation curriculum at DePaul University in Chicago.

headline: Private, Assurance Services, Partner at PwC US
about:
Lisa’s perseverance and tenacity are evident in what she sets out to accomplishment – whether it is completing the Breast Cancer 3 day walk despite serious physical injuries to both feet or taking companies public, clients can expect that she is fully engaged and committed to seeing things through.    Considered a go-to for her technical knowledge, her impact is built on the power of deep, connected relationships.  Compelled to help others, she has a passion for giving and seeing them succeed.  Others know that through her calm, collaborative and approachable nature, she is committed to her clients and teams having their best interests at heart.  Lisa is proud to be an Audit partner with PwC, leveraging thought leadership and leading clients through tough technical issues by listening, understanding their ultimate goals and quickly guiding them to resolution.

Lisa inspires by example as a leader and working mother of a child with disabilities.  Her strong Atlanta roots make her proud to be a home-grown female public company audit partner.  In addition to being a champion for her clients and team, as the mother of a child with differing abilities, she is an advocate for raising awareness of the power of diverse abilities in the workplace.   She has most recently been featured in Working Mother’s Magazine, regarding work-life balance, and the Chicago Tribune, discussing the PwC Disability Caregivers Network in the US, which she leads. She loves helping others who suddenly find themselves on this tough road of being a working parent of a child with special needs.  Lisa is also a member and past President of the Board of Directors for CURE Childhood Cancer and aims to help cure childhood cancer in her lifetime.  

Lisa enjoys meeting and connecting with new people in the community.

With almost 15 years' experience at PwC, she has held various leadership roles, including leading service teams for many of PwC's largest clients, with a focus on the technology, media and telecommunications (TMT) and private equity (PE) sectors. 

Office Managing Partner: Vanessa is the Office Managing Partner for PwC's NY office. As the face of the firm to the local community and businesses, she is passionate about driving market-driven corporate responsibility initiatives and delivering value to clients. She believes in providing pragmatic solutions balanced with creative flexibility to save clients time and money. She is equally passionate about all aspects of firm-wide activities, including people, community and workplace management.

Deals and Private Equity: In her role as Cyber Risk and Reg's (CRR) Deals Solution Lead and PE CRR Platform Lead, Vanessa ensures that clients receive expert guidance and advice to maximise deal value and reduce transaction risk. By focusing on the technology and digital aspects of a transaction, Vanessa advances her clients' objectives as they undertake complex, global integrations, divestitures, separations and joint ventures. Her clients value approaches that accelerate risk identification and mitigation strategies to achieve desired deal synergies and increase shareholder value.

Transformation, XaaS, Analytics & Automation: Vanessa has also worked with clients undergoing complex business transformations, advising them on the cross-functional implications specifically related to their business processes, systems and controls. Vanessa has also led the analysis of data at scale, including big data analysis, data validation and visual analytics. She also leads system implementations, particularly for solutions that support revenue growth through subscription and consumption business models and the new leasing standard. 

In addition, Vanessa has extensive and broad assurance experience in areas such as SEC, technical accounting, financial and operational controls, internal audit and compliance. She is a national speaker at various forums. She is a Certified Public Accountant in NY and a Fellow of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. projects.title: Global Consulting Challange: Champions
projects.description:
USC Marshall MBA students won the Overall Challenge and Company Segment of the 2016 Global Consulting Challenge, held March 3-4 at Google, Inc. headquarters in Mountain View. The five-member case competition team created a plan to transform the internal audit process, which has direct applicability to every internal audit department today, through use of data analytics.

"As the faculty adviser for the team, I am pleased to report that our students offered a big, bold and sophisticated platform,” said Suh-Pyng Ku, vice dean for graduate programs and professor of clinical finance and business economics. “Effectively, they built a rocket ship."

“I know I speak for the entire team when I say that the GCC was the most difficult and rewarding part of our business school experience,” said Michael Kohl MBA ’17, who served as team captain. “Everyone from our professors to our classmates to the MBA program staff contributed to this victory. We could not have done this without the support of our Trojan family.”

The Global Consulting Challenge is a 14-year-old invitation-only case competition that draws teams from leading business schools around the globe. It is usually held at USC's University Park Campus. This year, however, Google invited USC Marshall to host the competition at its campus.

Teams had three weeks to delve into complex, hypothetical data sets from Google and prepare presentations for three judging panels. Teams did not reveal their school affiliations until after the judging.

USC Marshall was one of nine teams competing. Participating business schools included Chicago Booth, Copenhagen Business School, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), IESE, MIT Sloan, Northwestern Kellogg, NYU Stern and Yale.

about:
I bring over 20 years of experience helping my clients transform their organizations and connect value and human capital within the context of a transaction -- acquisition, divestiture, carveouts, etc.  I have broad expertise encompassing HR, culture, change management, communications, talent management & retention, and leadership alignment across both private equity and corporate clients and the industrial products & services, Energy, and Power and Utilities industries. 

My reputation, however, is based on my ability to equip and empower my teams with the right tools and techniques that liberate existing organizational intelligence, insight, wisdom and talent. 

As a change champion, I believe in the thought shared by Dr. Travis Bradberry: “Managers light a fire under people. Leaders light a fire in people.” Leading by example is the surest way to building trusting relationships and creating a picture of what's possible. 

The greatness of a community is proportional to the compassionate actions of its members. projects.title: A Symmetric Key Cryptosystem using Transcendental Numbers
projects.description:
This project was done as my final year B.E dissertation. Around the time I started this project, vulnerabilities of AES cipher were exposed, and many blogs were being written on it. 
My project was to extend Rijndael Cipher (AES) and make it more secure by fixing the vulnerabilities in same computational time.

I observed that the decimal expansion of Transcendental numbers are completely random. By exploiting this mathematical phenomenon, the S-Box in AES was randomised after each round. My algorithm builds new S-Box at the end of each round and encrypts the data.

Finally the Transcendental number, decimal place from which S-box was randomised and a private key are used in the new algorithm, which takes the security of AES cipher to whole new level.

slides.title: Light up someone’s world: Encouraging others to use cameras during virtual meetings
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: One unforeseen consequence of the new way of working is the expectation that we’re all joining virtual meetings. No matter where we are, or how many meetings we’ve joined in the past, they’re always stressful. If you’re anything like me, I’m always wondering, “Will I look alright? What if my pets appear in the background? What if I need to get up in the middle of a call?” These are all valid questions, but to make sure you and others get the most out of your meeting, it's important to stay visible and appear engaged. Here are a few tips to help you use your camera and encourage others to do so. Set a trend: Join the call a few minutes early and turn your camera on. As others join, they’ll see your example and be encouraged to do the same. Use introductions creatively: Many people are afraid to turn cameras on because they’re embarrassed about their backgrounds. To remedy this, tell your participants what they might see in the background as an introduction. For example: “Hi, I’m Daniel, and today you might see my guitar behind me, I’ve been a terrible player since high school.” Then repeat the exercise with others--this will put them at ease with what’s behind them and set a conversational tone for the rest of the meeting Acknowledge the fact you’re at home, and you can’t control what’s happening. As with the background example, set a tone for this with everyone upfront in an introduction. For example: “Hi, I’m Daniel, I’m expecting a package from Amazon any minute, so please forgive me if you hear a doorbell and puppies barking.” Set the tone for your meeting by acknowledging the elephant in the room: that you're at home and can't control what's happening around you. For longer meetings, use spotters: A spotter is a member of your team who monitors a meeting and reports who’s paying attention, or who’s off camera to presenters and facilitators. If you know of 2-3 critical audience members, have your spotter pay close attention to them, and send you updates of what they’re doing in an offline chat. Then, as appropriate, call on them, or conduct an energizer exercise to bring the group together if they’re tuning out. Match your tone: Put your audience at ease by showing you're in a similar situation to them, and that you understand their challenges by matching your style and expectations to what's possible for them. Research your audience and determine their individual circumstances. For example, if you know someone has small children at home, don't pressure them to be on camera. Accordingly, try to match your clothing, accessories, and appearance to your audience. In an example, if you know your primary participants are casual, wear less formal clothing. Look, sound, feel your best: Nothing will engender confidence like knowing you’ve done all you can do to look and sound you best on camera. Invest in a high quality webcam and microphone. Don't rely on your built in laptop devices. When it’s time to be on screen, try to place your face in the center of the shot. This will help minimize the appearance that you’re towering over the screen, and show that you’re engaged and ready to listen. Show you’re interested: It’s disheartening to see others not paying attention. Do all you can to combat this by keeping your eyes on the camera, and not multitasking. Make eye contact with the camera at all times. It may be tempting to look at your participants as you speak, but doing so will make your eyes shift. Instead, place your eyes on your camera, and try not to look away when you’re speaking. Rely on your spotter to monitor the virtual room and give you feedback. Likewise, when a critical audience member is speaking, or you’re being addressed, look into the camera. This shows you’re engaged, and tells their spotter that you’re a VIP. Finally, while we all adjust to a new way of working it’s entirely natural to feel uncomfortable with these ways of connecting. However, remember, it’s entirely likely your audience feels the same way. So don't be afraid to smile, to laugh, and to try new things. After all, we’re all in this together, and in doing so, you might just bond with your audience in new ways.

slides.title: Keeping Control: Managing Virtual Meetings
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: Earlier this week we explored some general ideas about working, and managing projects, from home. A huge part of this is managing virtual meetings, calls, and teleconferences. In over 10 years, I’ve led more virtual collaborations than I can count, working with professionals from 6 continents. It’s not always easy, but here are some ideas to help: Get your tech ready All of these tips mean nothing if you can’t connect to the office. Be sure your laptop and phone are charged up, your VPN is working, and your teams have a strong collaboration space. Also test out microphones before meetings, making sure you don’t have too much background noise, and try out your camera keeping an eye on how you look, and also what’s in the background. Speak slowly and enunciate Keep in mind your audience might be outside, or surrounded by noise. Make sure everyone can clearly understand you at all times by talking slower than a normal conversation, and projecting your voice, even if it’s just into a headset. Stay visible If possible, share your screen and use your camera during virtual meetings, this helps others get a sense of who you are, and also keeps them focused on the items being presented. Share an agenda, and ask questions in advance Keeping a virtual meeting in order starts by sharing the reason for why it’s happening in the first place. Make sure every meeting has a clear agenda, with speaking roles mapped to each agenda item. Share this well in advance of each meeting, and again 10-15 minutes before the meeting if practical. This helps keep teams focused, and also helps you end detailed conversations that could be taken offline. Come to virtual meetings with an overly positive attitude TV anchors are told to exaggerate their emotions; the same is true for anyone on a virtual meeting. The tone you set as the leader of a virtual meeting generally determines its outcome. Arrive at each call early, prepared with an agenda, and with an overly positive attitude. Your colleagues can’t see you, so all they have to go by is the tone of your voice. Staying upbeat will motivate them, and help keep them focused. Hold daily team meetings, even for 15 minutes Not everyone is going to be engaged on every project every day, but you don’t want them to forget your project. Set aside a daily touchpoint with your colleagues, if only to say “good morning.” People are more likely to ask questions on the phone than take the time to write an e-mail. Your quick time to ask how things are going can mean the difference between a project moving along, or falling behind. At the same time, it helps your team feel engaged, and establishes you as a leader who’s interested in their success and the project’s objectives, helping them realize they can come to you with concerns. Take roll, or use a tool that does it for you It’s critical to make sure you have the right audience, and that others are aware of who’s with them on a call. At the onset of each call, ask all attendees to announce themselves, and run down this list before getting started. This not only helps others feel included, it positions you as the first speaker, letting you control the agenda. Use a tracker Since you can’t look across the room, or pop into a colleague’s office to check on status, it’s critical to stay on top of action items. Building a tracker to monitor progress is an excellent way to stay organized. Using a spreadsheet, start by listing all RFP requirements, assigning an owner, due date, and keeping a running list of notes related to each line. You can also add in lines for other open items, but ensure all items are tied back to some measure of customer compliance and responsiveness. This is another great place to consolidate your writer’s sheets and client hot button issues, as specified by APMP. Prioritize meeting items For virtual meetings, timing and scope creep are productivity killers. Since you can’t read the room, you can’t easily control what happens. Combat this by sending an agenda for each meeting, and following it to the letter. When reviewing progress on a document, don’t share the draft Many times a virtual review session is derailed because one person isn’t happy with the color of a graphic, or the font in a particular section. Combat this scope creep by only sharing your tracker on your screen during meetings, and encouraging your team to follow along in the document on their own screens. This helps them focus only on what’s required at that moment, while minimizing the risk of your call descending into chaos. Be clear with follow up items, and over communicate After each meeting, share follow up items immediately, and ensure all follow up asks clearly specify timing, ownership, and escalation pathways. At the same time, remember that teams generally respond better to simple tasks with short deadlines. This helps empower a team to understand what’s expected of them, and helps them think of potential bottlenecks or areas where they may require additional support. While virtual meetings have never been called easy, they don’t have to be painful. Taking the time to plan ahead will help empower your teams, and make you an e-meeting superstar in no time. Want to learn more about managing proposals, and how to get the most out of your team? Follow me on LinkedIn and check out my latest book, Preparing for a Shift: How Millennials will Redefine the Proposal Industry on Amazon

slides.title: The New Normal: Adjusting to Managing Proposals From Anywhere
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: As humans, we’re social animals. The need to connect is hardwired into each of us. For those of us in the bid and proposal industry, this drive for connection is even stronger. Think of all the bonds that are made in a war room, all the nuance that goes into driving a team towards successfully building a complex bid. Now try to do this without the benefit of seeing your colleagues face to face. It’s a hard skill to master, but one we’ve learned. I’ve supported thousands of bids, working remotely for over 10 years. With all of us working virtually for at least a few weeks, here are some practical ideas to help you get the most out of your teams while you can’t be in the office. Set clearly defined start and end times The hardest part about working from home is managing your time. Believe it or not, it’s not getting motivated that’s tough, it’s quitting at the end of the day. While at the office you can walk out the door and leave your work for tomorrow, this isn’t possible when working from home. To fight burnout, try to start your day at roughly the same time every morning, and set a clear end time for when you’ll walk away from your computer. Keep rituals alive Staying plugged in and motivated comes from maintaining what worked well for you in the office. If you start every day with a danish and coffee from the corner bakery, have the same breakfast in your kitchen before going heads down into work. Create a separate work space At the end of a stressful day, isn’t it nice to walk out of the office and leave that part of your life behind you? To the extent possible do the same when working from home. Try to set up a separate room, or a place in your home that’s only dedicated to work, and do as much of your work there as possible. Also, tell your kids and significant other to keep their distance from this space, as you need to be fully engaged during work hours. This not only keeps you focused by minimizing distractions, but it also keeps work turmoil from becoming a part of your home and limits the impact of your being there to your family. Respect boundaries Boundaries not only apply to how you handle working from home, but how you interact with others who are doing the same. As mentioned above, start by dedicating as separate a space as you’re able to be your dedicated workstation. Have discussions with your family or those who live with you about your working hours, and establish times when you’re not to be disturbed. Share the outcomes of these conversations with your leadership and teams, and ask the same of them. By setting boundaries up front, you set expectations, minimizing the chances of confusion and last minute crises. For example, if you need to make dinner for your kids from 4PM - 6PM every day, communicate to your teams that you’ll be offline at this time during kickoff, and discuss coverage options. Make time away from work Whatever you do, don’t let work bury you, and don’t isolate. To the extent it’s currently possible, maintain your normal work hours, and take time to keep on doing the things you’d normally do. Get away from your desk between meetings, and get outside as much as you can. Staying active is critical to keeping your motivation levels high. Control your own calendar To the extent you can, set your own invites when you're working from home. While you need to respect your customer’s needs, doing this for non essential or internal meetings helps minimize the chance you’ll be working off hours. Also, carefully evaluate how long you need meetings to last. Many times, what takes an hour in person can be done in 30 minutes on the phone by sharing materials and asking questions in advance. Make time to connect, and find new ways to do it Time with your colleagues doesn’t have to be all work and no play, Find ways to stay connected, and share in each other's lives. Some ideas include starting a book club, and having a video conference session to discuss what you’ve read, or hosting a video watch party on social media. Also, send work anniversary and birthday notes, and be sure to recognize any successes virtually just like you’d do in the office. Get your tech ready All of these tips mean nothing if you can’t connect to the office. Be sure your laptop and phone are charged up, your VPN is working, and your teams have a strong collaboration space. Also test out microphones before meetings, making sure you don’t have too much background noise, and try out your camera keeping an eye on how you look, and also what’s in the background. Practice self care Working from home is hard. This might be the first time in decades you’ve been asked to do this, and it’s ok if it feels overwhelming. Nobody is perfect at this, and we will all learn from the progress we’re making. But look at each day as an opportunity to work from home a little bit better, and understand that many others are in the same place as you are right now. Enjoy the flexibility Want to have lunch at 11AM on your patio? Feel like walking the dog when the sun’s out at 3 in the afternoon. Go ahead! It’s ok to step away if you’re caught up. Make the most of this time and take care of things you would have never done at the office. Just make sure you’re prioritizing work, have the right approvals, and take your phone with you. In the end, working from home can be as exciting as it is gratifying. Just be sure to set clear boundaries and expectations, communicate with your colleagues, and take care of yourself along the way. You may find this new way of working is just right for you! Want to learn more about managing proposals, and how to get the most out of your team? Follow me on LinkedIn and check out my latest book, Preparing for a Shift: How Millennials will Redefine the Proposal Industry on Amazon

headline: Deals Manager at PwC, CPA
about:
✦ Summary ✦

A CPA with 7+ years of client-facing experience at PwC, I’ve supported both private equity and corporate clients across financial due diligence and audit engagements. My background spans financial due diligence analysis, audit execution, and cross-functional collaboration across a range of industries and business models. I’ve worked with companies ranging from early-stage growth to large multinational corporations—each presenting its own set of financial structures, operating models, and complexities.

I began my career in PwC’s Audit and Assurance group, where I led audit work for Fortune 500 clients in the automotive, consumer products, and business services sectors. That experience built a strong foundation in technical accounting, internal controls, and financial statement risk assessment. Since transitioning into PwC’s Deals practice, I’ve supported over 20 buy-side and sell-side transactions across manufacturing, technology, and healthcare. My work focuses on helping clients assess the quality of earnings, understand working capital and debt-like items, and identify key risks and performance drivers to inform investment decisions.

In my current role as a Manager in the Financial Due Diligence team, I lead engagements from kickoff through delivery, coordinate closely with cross-functional teams, and support senior stakeholders throughout the diligence process. I enjoy navigating the complexity of financial data, drawing insights that bring clarity to the deal process, and helping clients move forward with confidence.

✦ Key Achievements ✦

▸ Led and supported 20+ financial due diligence engagements for private equity and corporate clients, involving businesses with EBITDA ranging from under $100K to over $200M
▸ Managed cross-functional workstreams (including tax, HR, and operations) and led daily communication with internal and external stakeholders
▸ Reviewed earnings and net working capital analyses, normalized financial results, and prepared client deliverables including databooks and executive-ready reports
▸ Gained experience across a range of sectors including manufacturing, consumer products, technology, healthcare, and business services

Please feel free to contact me at cunhamorrie@gmail.com.

headline: Manager - Consulting at PwC
about:
I am currently an Manager in the Operations Consting practice at PwC with a focus in the Digital Solutions group, primarily servicing clients in the Insurance sector. 

Since joining this practice in Jan 2018, I have advised large life and annuity providers through multi-year digital transformation programs by providing program management, change management, program governance, business analysis, data analytics, quality assurance and support. 

Prior to Jan 2018, I spent a year in PwC’s Deals practice advising clients through complex financial reporting issues arising from both sell-side and buy-side transactions in the insurance space, see below for notable experiences.

publications.title: Fabrication of Micro-Batteries via Stop-Flow Lithography
publications.description: Fabrication of micro-MEM devices and stretchable wearable electronics is important for future applications in materials, medicine and drug delivery. A key challenge in this area is the fabrication of rechargeable micro batteries with thicknesses < 500 μm, area < 0.1 mm2, energy densities of at least 1 to 10μWh cm-2 μμm-1. The overarching aim of this project is to develop a robust platform to fabricate micro batteries by combining double emulsion generation to fabricate porous microspheres that will serve as the anode and cathode materials and stop-flow lithography in microfludic devices to assemble the battery internals in a single step. In this presentation, I will discuss the tasks performed to assemble the stop flow lithography system, and the generation of active materials from double emulsions. The tasks include: (1) setting up the shutter and solenoid as well as syncing their operation, (2) fabricated masks for micro-particles by electric cutter and printing method, (3) performed trials to fabricate particles of different sizes and shapes, and (4) fabricated and operated double emulsion devices. The work accomplished during the summer serves as a strong foundation for the rest of the project.

about:
Marty Collins is a Partner in PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP Washington National Tax Services Office.   In his role, Marty works with client service teams for several of the Firm's premier clients as an international tax partner.

Marty's practice covers a wide-range of cross-border tax issues, including analyzing developments and identifying planning opportunities arising from new tax legislation (2017 Tax Reform), regulations and treaties.  Much of Marty’s work emanates from his clients’ acquisitions, dispositions or business expansions.
 
Marty specializes in advising clients on structuring tax-efficient acquisition and disposition structures, cross-border reorganizations including section 7874 (inversion) considerations, inbound financing structures, cross-border joint ventures, and principal/entrepreneur structures.  Marty's practice includes developing and analyzing strategies for tax-efficient IP, financing and holding-company structures, including strategies for the redeployment of foreign earnings.  Marty regularly advises clients on the U.S. anti-deferral (e.g., Subpart F income and GILTI), overall foreign loss, and foreign tax credit rules and regulations.

Marty frequently speaks and writes on a broad range of international tax issues.

Marty joined PricewaterhouseCoopers in 1995 in Baltimore; transferred to Washington National Tax Services from 1998 to 2003; transferred to Chicago from 2003 to 2005; and then rejoined in March 2008 from McDermott Will & Emery where he was a partner in that firm’s tax practice from 2005-2008.

about:
I have worked in international tax services at PwC since receiving a full-time offer while at Ohio State University. I work with a variety of teams, both internal and external to PwC, on projects covering general international tax concepts, technical international tax concepts, mergers & acquisitions, and transfer pricing. I have a wide breadth of coverage in these subject matter areas, in addition to experience working with other tax, accounting, and financial matters.

I have experience acting in a manager capacity where I have team(s) working under my supervision and have been afforded extensive opportunities to work in a project-manager capacity, with cross-functional teams outside of tax.

My client base has been diverse and I have a working knowledge of the pharmaceutical, biomedical, and industrial and specialized manufacturing industries, along with a moderate level of experience working with private equity clients.

Beyond the skills I've acquired while working as an international tax professional at PwC, I have a robust level of knowledge and interest in the sports industry. I have demonstrated an ability both within my career as a tax professional and outside of it that I have an affinity for innovation and finding new ways to add value and create efficiencies. These examples are prevalent in my career where routine tasks on various projects I've worked on have been automated or reimagined in order to optimize resource deployment.

The vast majority of my career has been spent on team-based engagements where I collaborate with upper-management and lower-staff levels and have been responsible for communicating project findings, results, and presentations in client-facing environments and for high-level, industry-wide, partner-facing meetings and summits.

Overall, I've shown capabilities in performing within a team-setting and managing both the people that work under my supervision, and also perform under the supervision of those those above me. Given the breadth of my diverse client-base and projects I've had the opportunity to work on, I have a tremendous understanding of different working styles and industries and can be flexible in adapting to any environment I find myself. I have lived overseas and have an appreciation for both work and non-work cultures across the globe, which has only been elevated due to my career in international tax. about:
My approach to business leadership and strategic differentiation can be summarized as ‘customer inspired.’ It’s a consistent theme throughout my career—whether advising Fortune 500 companies on how to create value, launching and running two successful businesses, or leading transformative initiatives at PwC.

Currently, I serve as the strategy leader for the launch of two cutting-edge digital innovation centers. These centers are designed to showcase PwC’s digital and technology capabilities, bringing clients into immersive environments where innovation meets problem-solving. From vision to execution, I help shape the strategy, content, and experiences that will define these centers and elevate PwC’s brand in the digital space.

Previously, as PwC’s Client Experience Strategy Leader, Assurance Experience Leader, and Client Listening Director, I spearheaded initiatives that redefined how we engage with clients. I leveraged data-driven insights to help leaders enhance loyalty, make customer-driven decisions, and embed a culture of delivering exceptional client experiences.

Beyond PwC, I’ve built and advised businesses across industries. I’ve founded and operated two successful companies, including an early IT company and a world-renowned Brazilian Jiu Jitsu academy. I’ve also worked as an agent/manager for a Hall of Fame athlete and continue to mentor entrepreneurs on strategy and growth.

Outside of business, I bring the same strategic mindset and competitive drive to Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, where I am an internationally decorated competitor with four Pan American Championships and a Brazilian National Championship.

At my core, I am passionate about helping organizations and individuals unlock new possibilities—whether through business transformation, customer experience innovation, or personal growth.

I am a software engineer with expertise in machine learning, data engineering, and distributed systems. I have experience building systems that integrate ML models into applications. My experience spans full-stack development, backend engineering, and ML model deployment, enabling me to bridge the gap between software engineering and AI.

At my most recent role in a fast-paced AI startup, I worked on object detection and pose estimation models, optimizing them for deployment on edge devices using OpenVINO and Docker. I built event-driven architectures to integrate ML models into production systems, enabling real-time report generation. 

Previously, at MasterCard, I leveraged big data technologies (Spark, Hadoop) to build ML-driven forecasting models for location insights. My work also included customer segmentation using clustering algorithms and automating data validation pipelines for large-scale datasets.

During my time at the University of Chicago, I designed and implemented ETL pipelines and ML models for student retention analysis, using classification and clustering techniques to identify key factors influencing admissions decisions.

During my Master's, I made AWS apps, implemented GPU algorithms and wrote several multi-threaded programs in C, GoLang, Python. I designed an auction website using microservices, designed my very own cache system and created a parallel image processing package in GoLang.

projects.title: Deception Detection using Machine Learning
projects.description: This dissertation describes work on deception detection in text, speech and video using machine learning techniques. Deception detection has been a study of interest in various domains like forensics, psychology, computer science and linguistics. It has promising applications in real life as the human counterparts are poor at detecting lies. This work examines the ability to deceive for different types of questions: Leading questions and open-ended questions, positive assumptions and negative assumption questions, outcome and process questions, recollection and hypothetical questions. This dissertation shows that video processing techniques and speech processing techniques can be applied to the domain of deception to extract useful features for classification. We also looked at the personality factors using the big five personality test and checked its impact on deception detection ability. An important product of this work is a balanced video and audio data set simulating a job interview. Results show that supervised classification models like K nearest neighbours classifier and support vector classifier can classify text and audio data to some success: The accuracy is better than human hearers and chance. Long short-term machines are used to classify the video data after facial feature extraction leading to test accuracy of 64.7%.
